subject: english-literature
title: Post-Colonialism and Said
welcome_lead: From Orientalism to subaltern voices — survey the post-colonial critical school.
meta_desc: Post-colonial theory — Said, Spivak, Bhabha — at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have walked the post-colonial corridor — empire's archive read against itself.

concepts.def: Edward Said (1978) — Western knowledge of 'the East' produces and supports imperial power.
Post-colonial critics analyse how Western texts construct non-European peoples as different and inferior.
Gayatri Spivak — those outside hegemonic discourse; her essay 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988) questions their representation.
Homi Bhabha — the in-between space where colonial cultures mix and resist.
Bhabha — colonised subjects imitate the coloniser, producing a partial, destabilising likeness.
Post-colonial writers (Achebe, Rhys, Walcott) rewrite canonical texts from the margins.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Said's Orientalism showed how a vast Western archive — novels, paintings, scholarship — constructed 'the Orient' as Europe's exotic and inferior counterpart.

Knowledge was inseparable from imperial power.
Spivak's essay (1988) interrogated whether subaltern voices can be heard within colonial archives. Even sympathetic intellectuals risk speaking for rather than with.

Bhabha's The Location of Culture (1994) theorised the in-between space of colonial encounters — hybrid, ambivalent, productive of resistance.

Mimicry — the colonised's partial imitation of the coloniser — both reproduces and destabilises authority.
